column2: Epilogue
Tea glowed golden in a white bone-china cup. Beside it, a small matching plate held scones sprinkled with rosewater.
In the principal’s office at Cassell College, Lu Mingfei and Principal Anjou were having afternoon tea across a broad desk.

An invitation to tea with the principal was an honor more coveted at Cassell than a scholarship. Unfortunately, Lu Mingfei was wrapped in gauze like a rice dumpling, with only his darting eyes visible, rather like the chainsaw-wielding zombie lady in Resident Evil. He hardly felt dressed for afternoon tea himself.
“A fine English tradition handed down from the Victorian era,” the principal said. “Try the second-flush Darjeeling. It’s excellent.”

Lu Mingfei lifted the bone-china cup, took a sip, and looked around. The principal’s office stood not far from Valhalla, an inconspicuous two-story building surrounded by trees. From outside it looked as plain as a garage, but the interior was another matter altogether.

The whole room was a bookcase. The first and second floors opened into each other beneath a huge frosted-glass skylight, still covered with leaves from last autumn. The afternoon sun felt wonderfully warm on Lu Mingfei. Oil paintings and bookcases reached to the ceiling on all four walls, the shelves filled with sets of hardbound books and reproductions of ancient texts. Stairs and platforms ran along the shelves at different heights, allowing people to climb up and down inside this enormous bookcase of a house.
“Do you like my office?” The principal looked pleased with himself.
“Mm.” Lu Mingfei nodded.

“A 4.0 GPA for your first semester. Here is your official transcript. I kept my promise. Congratulations. Not many people in Cassell’s history have earned full marks in their practicum.” The principal slid an envelope across the desk. His adviser Guderian’s elaborate signature crossed the seal.
“What did people do for the practicum before?”

“It depended. If a dragon happened to awaken, they would be assigned to an operation. Otherwise, they might excavate dragon ruins. And if there really was nothing to arrange, they could volunteer at the Chicago zoo’s crocodile pool and study reptilian evolution while they were at it.” The principal smiled. “You were lucky to have such an opportunity. But you still need to write a practicum paper. I’ve thought of a title for you: A Brief Analysis of the Four Monarchs of the Dragons.”
“That sounds incredibly profound... I’m afraid I won’t be able to write it.”

“It needn’t be very scholarly. Through practical experience you proved two things. First, the Four Monarchs mentioned in the Ice Sea Fragments do exist. They are first-generation dragons, the first generation sired by the Black King Nidhogg himself. Second, ‘twins sit upon the throne’: the King of Bronze and Fire was actually a pair of brothers.” The principal sighed. “A world-shaking discovery. If I could publish it, I’d have won a Nobel Prize by now.”
“You make it sound so academic... It was really just manual labor.” Lu Mingfei scratched his head.
“I can see you have questions. Ask.” The principal leaned forward on his elbows and looked at him.
Lu Mingfei thought for a moment, then raised his head. “Why... do Dragon Kings look human?”

The principal nodded. “You probably thought dragon slaying meant killing a great monster. Dragons can indeed take human form, but they remain another species. Their understanding of the world is entirely different from ours. We cannot regard them as human.”

A large envelope was handed to Lu Mingfei. He opened it, his hand trembling slightly. Inside was a photograph of Old Tang playing cards at a table with a group of people. They were in a cafe; sunlight streamed through floor-to-ceiling windows, brightening Old Tang’s young face.

“His real name was Ronald Tang. He was a Chinese American, adopted as a child. No one knows who his biological parents were. He dropped out of high school, lived in a poor neighborhood in Brooklyn, New York, and earned money taking secret jobs,” the principal said quietly. “We actually had his information before you left. We didn’t tell you because we knew you had met online.”
“How did he become a Dragon King?”

“He didn’t become one. He always was one. According to the Ice Sea Fragments, the brothers lived in a bronze palace in northern Europe. But after a certain year before the Common Era, we can find no further record of them. Now it seems they crossed the Eurasian continent to China. We don’t know how long the migration took. When they arrived, Wang Mang had usurped the Han throne, and China was at war. The elder brother took the name Li Xiong and used the power of dragons to gain the trust of Gongsun Shu, a warlord who held Sichuan. He urged Gongsun Shu to proclaim himself emperor and became one of his chief ministers.”
“Why did they do that?” Lu Mingfei asked.

“We don’t know. They must have had an important purpose, but no one knows it now. Twelve years later, apparently with the help of certain dragon-slaying families, Emperor Liu Xiu defeated Gongsun Shu and the brothers. At the moment before death, they completed the cocooning of their souls. The jar wasn’t a bone vessel at all, but an ‘egg’ in which a Dragon King could breed a new body. They hatched at different times. The younger brother developed more slowly; the elder left the egg first, but failed to recover his memories. He looked a little over twenty, though he may actually have been much older. He left before the Three Gorges Reservoir was built. Somehow he ended up in America and was adopted. For more than twenty years he lived there as a human, convinced that he was human, until his brother awakened later and awakened him.”
“You’re guessing all this?”
“Only an inference. They’re dead now. No one will ever know their story.”
“Aren’t dragons unable to die?”

“Usually. A high-ranking dragon can hatch again as long as it prepares an egg and cocoons its soul before death. Where that egg is hidden is the dragons’ greatest secret,” the principal said. “But this time was different. Norton never once tried to cocoon himself. He chose to merge with his dragon servitor. If he had succeeded, he could have unleashed the most powerful fire Yanling known to date: Torch Dragon.”
“What does Torch Dragon do?” Lu Mingfei asked.

“We don’t know. Sequence number 114, an extremely unstable Yanling. We believe that the last time Norton used it, he destroyed White Emperor City. Historians have never been certain where the city stood, because the original White Emperor City was destroyed by Torch Dragon shortly after it was built.”
“He doesn’t sound very sorry for what he did... Did he hate humans that much?” Lu Mingfei remembered Old Tang’s final look—or rather, the Dragon King Norton’s.
By then he had no longer recognized him. Or perhaps, as the principal said, dragons were dragons. Once Norton recovered his memories, he would no longer regard him as a friend.

“He wanted revenge. Constantine also gave up cocooning to protect him, which meant he could never come back to life.” The principal sighed. “We never knew whether dragons felt brotherly affection, but apparently they do. It’s one of the rare ways they resemble humans.”
“I think... they had it pretty hard,” Lu Mingfei said softly.
The principal rose, walked behind Lu Mingfei, and patted his shoulder. “This is a war between two species. All of us took our sides from the very beginning.”

Lu Mingfei nodded and studied the photograph one last time, then put it back in the envelope and returned it. He didn’t want to keep the bright smile of a Dragon King who believed he was human. There was nothing imposing about that face. Even knowing he was a dragon, Lu Mingfei could stare as hard as he liked and still see no sign of it.
“We caused such a commotion in China. Didn’t we attract anyone’s attention?”

The principal shrugged. “We were lucky this time. There were no other boats nearby, and the steam blocked the view. But as our operations continue, I can’t be sure how much longer we can keep the secret. I only hope we can end this war before it reaches the front page.”
“Why keep it secret? Wouldn’t it be good if everyone helped slay dragons?”

“For thousands of years, the dragon-slaying families have refused to reveal these secrets. The reasons are complicated, but above all, perhaps no one wants to shake humanity’s understanding of the world.” The principal spread his hands. “Humans and dragons understand the world very differently. Humans have lived by their beliefs for many years. If those beliefs were shattered, no one knows what might happen. Oh, I have a letter here, sent from an unknown place. I think it will make you happier than a 4.0 GPA or an invitation to tea with the principal.”
He took an envelope from his pocket and set it in front of Lu Mingfei.

It was white, with no stamp or postmark. The flap bore a red wax seal, a very old-fashioned way to close a letter. On the front, graceful handwriting read: “Principal Anjou, please forward to Lu Mingfei.”
Lu Mingfei’s lips felt dry. His hand trembled as he reached for it.
Mingfei,
We received a copy of your transcript. You did very well, much better than your father and I did in our day.
I wish I could be beside you now, sitting on your hospital bed and holding your hand, asking our new young man for his autograph.

But I can’t. We have been doing this work for twenty full years, and there is little time left. If I leave now, it may be too late. I have been a very inadequate mother, but I think one day you will understand why I did this.
You have taken a wonderful first step. You will grow into a son who makes me proud, and you will understand us too.
I carried you for ten difficult months before you were born. During those ten months and the eighteen years since, every day I imagined what you would be like when you grew up.

I have set our reunion for the year you turn twenty-two, the year you graduate from Cassell College. Your father and I have planned for many years to attend your graduation and see our only son in his cap and gown.
We love you, always.
Mom
Qiao Weini

P.S. Your father has been sitting beside me watching me write and roasting a rabbit. His hands are covered in grease, so he can’t touch a pen. He dictated many things for me to write to you, but I thought they were all nonsense, so I won’t repeat them. There was only one sentence I thought worth passing on: “Son, you’re eighteen and grown up now... If you insist on getting a girlfriend, I suppose I can’t really stop you...”
Lu Mingfei folded the letter along its creases and put it back in the envelope, then tried to find a pocket in which to keep it. He found none, so he tucked it into the bandages over his chest.
“Everyone exists in the eyes of others,” the principal said, patting his shoulder. “Someone has been watching over you all along.”
“Mm.” Lu Mingfei nodded.

“One last thing.” The principal looked him in the eye. “Chapter fifteen, section four of Cassell College regulations: participants in an operation may not discuss its details with one another. Once an operation is over, everything is sealed in the archives. So the details you don’t wish to tell me... don’t tell anyone else either. All right?”
Lu Mingfei started. “What... details?”

“According to the report, Caesar’s Shkval torpedo killed the Dragon King Norton, but we found no remains. Chen Motong says she was attacked underwater by something believed to be Norton. Whether it was Norton or not, she was badly injured. So I wonder: if Chen Motong was attacked, how did you escape unharmed?” The principal spoke casually.
“But I don’t intend to ask,” he added. “Whether there are things we don’t know, or you have your own reasons for keeping silent, I personally trust you. So I won’t ask.”
“Okay. I understand.” Lu Mingfei stood and scratched his head.

As he watched him descend the stairs, the principal took a stack of white sheets from a folder. Page after page bore simple drawings like a child’s. On the last page the style abruptly changed: sharp, vivid, lifelike. It showed two boys, one tall and one short, sitting on a windowsill beneath hanging green vines, looking together toward a distant tower. The taller wore a school uniform; the shorter, an awkwardly formal suit and square-toed leather shoes. All four feet dangled outside the window.
“It’s been a long time,” the principal whispered to the drawing.
He took out a lighter, set the papers alight, and watched them slowly turn to ash in the fireplace.
In Room 303 of Dormitory Zone 1, Fingel typed a headline for the campus news site: “S-Rank Released from Hospital: The Mummy Returns.”
The accompanying photograph showed Lu Mingfei, wrapped from head to foot in bandages, sitting by a window and making an old-fashioned V sign.
“What kind of headline is that?” Lu Mingfei protested behind him.
“It’s a movie. The Mummy Returns, starring Brendan Fraser,” Fingel said without looking up. “There are hordes of mummies in it, and every one looks like you.”
“Get lost! You used my picture. Are you paying me or not?”
“I’ve made you a famous figure on campus. You ought to pay me. In Chinese terms, I’m this college’s most successful online promoter.”
“Bullshit!” Lu Mingfei snatched the mouse and scrolled down. The second-ranked story was “S-Rank’s First Operation: What Exactly Did He Do Underwater?”

“The whole thing says I was shaking with fear underwater. What kind of negative publicity is this?” Lu Mingfei glared, though his eyebrows were hidden under bandages. “Why isn’t there a single shot of me being heroic? Cameras always chase me when I’m at my worst!”
The photograph showed him curled in a corner of the cabin, face deathly pale, vomiting into a lunch box.
“I was just seasick! Is seasickness that strange?”

“We had a part-time reporter on the ship, and that’s all he got of you... A few others were even worse,” Fingel said. “But it’s working nicely. Your popularity is nearly up there with Caesar and Chu Zihang.”
“But Caesar’s stories are all cool like this!” Lu Mingfei scrolled farther. Number three was “Caesar Gattuso, the Dazzling Dictator.”

The photograph showed Caesar aiming a sniper rifle on deck, firelight tracing a perfect masculine silhouette against his black combat uniform. His ice-blue eyes and clenched jaw suggested either ruthlessness or resolve. Either way, it was the kind of picture that made girls scream.

“He certainly looks much better than you, but you’re pursuing different images. Caesar Gattuso has spent twenty years establishing himself as an aristocratic young master. You have to find another path! I can sum up the image I’ve devised for you in two words. The first is ‘strong’!”
“That sounds pretty good. What’s the second?” It was rare for anyone to call Lu Mingfei strong.
“‘Tacky’! Hopelessly tacky. Your image is... tacky and strong!”
“I’m going to buy a beer...” Lu Mingfei turned away.
“Get me one too,” Fingel said.
“One is enough. Once it’s empty, I’m smashing the bottle over your head!”
Someone knocked on the door.
“Who is it?” Lu Mingfei went to open it.

Their eyes met. Caesar’s ice-blue pupils betrayed no expression, and Lu Mingfei sucked in a breath. As a new member of the Student Council, he might not have been terrified to face its president, but Caesar wearing a towel around his head and an apron, with a steel knife in his hand, was another matter.
“Do you have any pepper?” Caesar asked. “If you do, I won’t have to go out and buy some.”

“Y-yes! We do!” Lu Mingfei nodded hastily. The dorm rooms had bathrooms and small kitchens. Although he and Fingel never actually cooked, they had salt and pepper to sprinkle in their tomato soup when they ordered late-night food.
Trembling, Lu Mingfei handed him the pepper. Caesar nodded politely and walked into the room opposite.

“What’s going on? What is this?” Lu Mingfei grabbed his head. “Doesn’t he live in that campus villa called Amber Hall? Did his family suddenly go bankrupt? Has he moved into an ordinary dorm and started cooking for himself?”
A metallic hiss came from the opposite room: a blade being drawn. Lu Mingfei flinched.

The door across the hall was open. He peered inside, and his worldview collapsed. Chu Zihang, president of the Lionheart Society, had drawn Murasame, the sword rarely absent from his side. Standing back-to-back with Caesar, he flexed his wrist, then brought the blade down with steady precision... slicing the salmon on the table in front of him.
Meanwhile Caesar deftly chopped tomatoes with one hand and sprinkled pepper into a boiling pot with the other.
Both were as expressionless as ever.

“Hell! Did I... travel to another world? A world where Caesar and Chu Zihang get along! They’re living together... and cooking together!” Lu Mingfei flashed back into his room and seized Fingel by the collar.
“You don’t know why?” Fingel was perfectly calm.
“No! How many heroes in those other-world novels know why they were transported?”

“The rooms were reassigned. They used to group students by year, but now they’ve mixed them up. Caesar and Chu Zihang may be sworn enemies in campus politics, but their girlfriends happen to share a room. Right across the hall from us: Room 304.”
“Girlfriends?” Lu Mingfei’s mind went blank.
“President! Have you sliced the ham I asked for? My pizza’s ready to go in the oven!” A girl in a checked apron came up the stairs carrying a baking tray lined with pizza dough.
She saw Lu Mingfei staring openmouthed, realized she had spoken too loudly, and immediately resumed her ladylike manner. Smiling with her lips pressed together, she slipped into the room opposite.
Lu Mingfei blinked. It felt as if flocks of little crows were flying over his head... flying... and flying...
He knew that pretty black-haired girl. He had even shot her once. She was Susie, who had ambushed Nono on Freedom Day.

“Vice president of the Lionheart Society, Susie. Chinese, third year, Nono’s longtime roommate. Rumor says she’s Chu Zihang’s secret girlfriend, though they’ve both denied it in public.” Fingel leaned against the wall, drinking a Coke. “As head of the campus news site’s entertainment section, I’m a pretty good gossip reporter.”
“Isn’t this a little too cozy?”

“Caesar and Chu Zihang do fight fiercely, but nobody said they have to draw swords and chop at each other every time they meet forever. Normally they probably wouldn’t do this, but today is White Day. The girls apparently didn’t want to go out, so Caesar and Chu Zihang had to put up with it.”
“White Day?”
“A holiday popular in Japan, March fourteenth. Girls give boys gifts in return,” Fingel said. “Have you ever received any chocolate?”
“No.” Lu Mingfei hung his head.
Valentine’s Day, Christmas, White Day—what were they all for? As a diehard member of the anti-romance brigade, Lu Mingfei hated them most of all.
“Then I’ll give you a piece,” someone said.
A pair of long, shapely legs entered his field of vision, ending in soft cork flip-flops. A red cord circled one ankle, with a jade pendant hanging from it.
He looked up and saw a silver four-leaf-clover pendant set with diamonds beside the girl’s ear, and a piece of chocolate wrapped in gold foil.
Nono wore short shorts and a close-fitting white T-shirt. She leaned against the opposite doorframe, bandages still wrapped around her.
Lu Mingfei rubbed his hands and grinned, baring his teeth.

Who had made the room assignments? How thoughtful could they be? For the first time in his life, a girl had given him chocolate on Valentine’s Day. Who cared whether the day was black or white? The chocolate had been handed to him by a long-legged girl in short shorts! Was this his luck finally turning? What incredible luck! No, romantic luck!
“It’s pretty good,” Nono said. “I’m not kidding.”
“Is there one for me?” Fingel asked.
“Oh,” Nono said. “Wait a second.”
She went back inside, then returned with a black-wrapped piece and handed it to Fingel.
“This is an important day!” Fingel clapped Lu Mingfei hard on the shoulder. “The first piece of chocolate a girl has ever given you!”
“Bullshit!” Lu Mingfei thought. “If you hadn’t barged in, mine would have meant so much more! What is this? Fingel and I got chocolate from the same girl?”
Even so, holding the chocolate, he felt happiness bubbling from every pore.
“You even bought different kinds. How thoughtful!” Fingel said.
“Nono, did you take apart the chocolate wall?” Susie called from inside.
“Mm. Caesar doesn’t eat chocolate. He only cared about spelling out his name with it, and he’s seen it already anyway.”
Fingel and Lu Mingfei peered into Room 304. A wall of chocolate as tall as a person stood there, built from gold and black pieces to spell Caesar’s name in English.
Two pieces had now been removed from one corner, which was propped up with a can of Coke.
“My heart is broken. Your love for me is less than one percent of your love for Caesar,” Fingel said.
“I can put you first on the waiting list of admirers,” Nono said.
While they talked, Lu Mingfei looked at the chocolate wall, scratched his head, stuck out his tongue, and turned toward his own room.
“Thank you,” Nono said behind him.
“Oh... you’re welcome.” Startled, he turned around.

He didn’t know what she was thanking him for. He had told the principal only part of what happened underwater; he couldn’t exactly say he had sold his soul or body, been possessed by a devil, and knocked out the Dragon King. Naturally, he hadn’t mentioned those English Yanling either. By that account, he should be thanking Nono, not the other way around.
“Aren’t you going to ask why?” Nono tilted her head at him.
“Fingel, can you come help me watch the pizza? You can have some when it’s ready,” Susie called from inside.
“No problem! Let me tell you, an eighth-year senior is far more reliable than those boys in the lower grades!” Fingel wriggled his way into Room 304.
Only Lu Mingfei and Nono remained in the empty hallway. He opened his mouth, intending to speak.
“Delivery for Lu Mingfei.” A security guard emerged from the stairwell.
Lu Mingfei signed the receipt. It was a large FedEx envelope, addressed from Britain. He weighed it in his hand, feeling something inside.
“Don’t tell me... another phone?” he thought. The large envelope and the feel of it were just like the first letter he had received from Cassell College.
He tore it open and tipped out... an iPhone.
“A Valentine’s gift?” Nono asked curiously.
Lu Mingfei was curious too. Nothing in the envelope identified the sender. The phone was half charged. Its contact list was empty, and its message list contained a single text from “Unknown Number.”
Dear Mr. Lu Mingfei,

From this moment on I shall regard you as a client. Thank you very much for your patronage. Our cooperation in the battle to eliminate the Dragon King Norton was a pleasure. I hope future collaborations will be just as enjoyable. (Note: I mean please summon me as often as possible so that we can complete our contract sooner.)

I know you have long lacked a suitable phone, so I give you this iPhone as a small gift and a convenient means of communication. Keep this message and reply directly; I will receive your request. Since I am not China Mobile, this messaging service is free. It will consume none of your soul... or body.
Now, as the price, I have taken one quarter of your life.
Lu Mingze
Today
The moment he finished reading, the screen switched to a new interface. An ancient bronze-colored dial spun rapidly.
As soon as Lu Mingfei’s finger touched the screen, the dial slowed. When it stopped, its scale read “75%.”
His palm was slick with cold sweat.
“Are you all right?” Nono asked.
Lu Mingfei hastily switched off the screen. “Why did you thank me?”
He didn’t want Nono to know about this, whether it was a prank or real.
“Because I probably would have died without you,” she said.
“What?” He stared.

“When I passed out, I was so tired. I wanted to go to sleep. But I could just barely hear you calling my name,” Nono said. “I hazily thought you must have been scared to death, or you wouldn’t have kept shouting.”
After a silence, Lu Mingfei nodded. “Yeah. Scared to death.”
“If you hadn’t called me, I would have fallen asleep. And probably never woken up. Thank you.”
“Oh... you’re welcome,” Lu Mingfei repeated.
“Because I promised to look after you, I thought I couldn’t go to sleep.” Nono frowned. “Don’t be annoying! You can’t keep saying ‘you’re welcome’ back and forth!”
“Uh... all right. I understand.”
So when someone promised to look after you, they could take it that seriously.
After all the silly nonsense and jokes he had spoken, when he could hardly tell which of his own words he meant, he had discovered that someone could be so serious.
Nono... was just a stubborn kid too.
He smiled and scratched his head. Nono smiled as well and reached over; together they mussed his hair into a bird’s nest.
“It’s fine. Everything’s fine...” Lu Mingfei looked up at Nono with a foolish grin. “Don’t worry.”
“I’m not worried.” Nono shrugged. “You just looked a little strange a moment ago. Want to have pizza with us? Lots more people are coming. It’s a party tonight.”
“I have something to do. I’ll go first.”
“See you, then.”
“See you.” Lu Mingfei turned away.
“Hey!” Nono called after him.
“What?” He looked back.
“Are you going to be noisy at night? Susie and I are both sensitive to noise.”
“Don’t worry. As long as I gag Fingel and stuff him under the covers, there won’t be a sound.”
“See that you do.” Nono went back inside.
Fingel was talking loudly to Susie in the room.
A buzz of voices rose from downstairs. The party guests were probably arriving.
Lu Mingfei rounded a corner and spat at the phone. “Pah! Bullshit! I haven’t lived enough yet. Sell you my life?”
He hesitated, wanting to hurl the phone through the window opposite, so that it would disappear somewhere even he couldn’t find it.
But in the end he switched it off and put it in his pocket.

“Lu Mingfei,” he whispered to himself, “all that authority and power... as long as you don’t touch it, you can keep on, forever and ever... living next door to the person you like. Isn’t that good enough?”
“Ha ha.”
A faint voice sounded somewhere far behind him, audible only to Lu Mingfei. It was a child’s laugh, impossible to tell whether kind or mocking.
Lu Mingfei’s diary:
April 23, 2010. Cassell College. Sunny, turning cloudy.
To put it simply, today was utterly unremarkable.

Two periods of Introduction to Dragon Genealogy, which felt a lot like high-school history; two of Magic-Powered Mechanical Design I, which sounds cool but is really mechanical drafting. In the evening, Alchemical Chemistry I lab: using a hydrogen flame to remove impurities from soda cans and refine pure aluminum. The damn lab teacher kept stressing that if the hydrogen cylinder exploded, it would punch through the floor like a pile driver, fly into the basement, and flatten itself against the hard ground into a sheet of steel—and we wouldn’t get to see the sheet, because we would undoubtedly all be dead. It scared me so much that my hand shook when I held the torch, and I accidentally burned Zero’s hair.
I promised to buy Zero lobster tails to apologize. If it costs a hundred dollars, my credit-card debt will be $4,850.45. Most of the money went to Fingel’s late-night meals.
This month’s scholarship hasn’t arrived because I forgot my Introduction to Dragon Genealogy homework. Professor Guderian won’t release it until I come to his office for a talk.
I really don’t want to go. He talks too much!
As long as my card still works, I’d better stay away from that nagging old man...
This is the second semester of my utterly unremarkable college life, and the unremarkableness will go on.
But today I passed the gym and saw Nono practicing ballet in a white dress!
A white ballet dress...
White ballet dress, bless me: no Alchemical Chemistry quiz tomorrow!
